Alisha is 38, works as retail salesperson, with partner or family.

What brings them here now. Alisha reports six weeks of feeling unable to keep up with the demands of an acting-lead role she took on at the store during a staffing shortage, on top of her regular shifts, alongside a two-year pattern of lower back pain that has flared with the longer hours on her feet. She is clear that nothing in her life has actually gone wrong — she denies any trouble with her relationship, her work performance, or her money, and insists customers and colleagues still see her as 'fine' — and she does not want to give the role up; she wants to do it and not be this depleted. She mentions the back only when asked, waving it off as 'everybody's got something,' though she connects it readily to how little she has left by Friday.
What they want out of support: I want to get through a workweek without feeling like I'm barely holding it together, and have enough left on a Saturday to open my sketchbook again.

Predisposing. Her back first started talking to her two years ago, after she muscled through a candle shipment alone on a short-staffed day — boxes down a ladder, no help until closing — and it never really went quiet again. She kept working full shifts on concrete floors, rotating between a heating pad, ibuprofen, and her mother's Epsom salts, and the one clinic visit got her ten minutes, a stretch sheet, and the news that nothing on the scan was anything anyone could fix. What those two years taught her was that the pain eases just often enough for her to believe it's over, and then comes right back. She got used to planning her days around it — which shoes, which aisle, where she'd sit on the bus — and somewhere in there she stopped expecting it to ever really end.

Precipitating. Six weeks ago, two days before the holiday reset, the store's assistant manager quit without notice, and Alisha was asked to run point — schedules, receiving, the reset itself — while still covering her own shifts on a floor that was already short. She said yes in the parking lot before she'd checked her calendar, because it's exactly the step toward assistant manager she's been working toward. Since then she's worked six-day weeks, rebuilt the schedule twice after call-outs, and caught herself forgetting vendor orders until the driver phoned her, while her back flared from the doubled hours on her feet. She's still the salesperson customers ask for by name, which is part of why nobody at the store sees what it's costing; last Tuesday she sat in the driveway for twenty minutes after getting home before she could make herself go inside.

Her way through is to keep everyone reassured and buy herself pockets of okay — an hour over the stove, a small purchase in a pretty bag — without letting anyone see how thin she's stretched.
